candidates.name: Mosaic of Subcultures
candidates.description: A healthy city is a mosaic of subcultures, not a homogeneous mass. Maps to microservices architecture, team topologies, and organizational diversity -- a system thrives when its parts maintain distinct identities rather than converging on uniformity.

candidates.name: Scattered Work
candidates.description: Work should be scattered throughout the community, not concentrated in one district. Prefigures distributed teams, remote work, and the argument against monolithic office campuses.

candidates.name: Identifiable Neighborhood
candidates.description: People need an identifiable spatial unit to belong to. Maps to team identity in organizations, namespace boundaries in code, bounded contexts in domain-driven design.

candidates.name: Network of Learning
candidates.description: Learning should happen in a decentralized network, not a centralized institution. Directly anticipates MOOCs, learning communities, and the 'bazaar' model of knowledge sharing.

candidates.name: Four-Story Limit
candidates.description: Buildings taller than four stories are inhumane -- they disconnect people from the ground. Maps to the argument against deep inheritance hierarchies, excessive abstraction layers, and the principle that systems should stay close to their foundations.

candidates.name: Sacred Sites
candidates.description: Some places have special meaning and should be preserved. Maps to legacy systems that must not be touched, sacred cows in organizations, and the principle that not everything should be refactored.

candidates.name: Activity Nodes
candidates.description: Concentrate activity at nodes where paths cross. Maps to API gateways, event hubs, and the organizational 'water cooler' -- places where serendipitous interaction generates value.

candidates.name: Degrees of Publicness
candidates.description: Spaces should transition gradually from public to private. Maps directly to access control models, API visibility levels (public/internal/private), and information classification hierarchies.

candidates.name: Work Community
candidates.description: Workplaces should be small enough that people know each other. Maps to two-pizza teams, Dunbar's number in organizations, and the scaling principle that large organizations should be composed of small autonomous groups.

candidates.name: Main Gateways
candidates.description: Mark the entrances to a building or neighborhood to create a sense of arrival. The API gateway pattern, login screens, and onboarding flows all implement this -- the threshold between outside and inside must be deliberate.

candidates.name: Quiet Backs
candidates.description: Every busy area needs a quiet refuge nearby. Maps to staging environments, sandbox modes, focus time in organizations, and the 'do not disturb' pattern in notification systems.

candidates.name: Accessible Green
candidates.description: Everyone needs access to open green space within walking distance. Maps to the argument for accessible shared resources -- commons, open-source libraries, shared infrastructure that everyone can reach without gatekeepers.

candidates.name: Master and Apprentices
candidates.description: The master-apprentice relationship is the most effective form of learning. Maps to pair programming, mentorship programs, and the argument that expertise transfers through proximity, not documentation.

candidates.name: Small Services Without Red Tape
candidates.description: Services should be small, local, and unbureaucratic. Directly anticipates the microservices philosophy, the Unix philosophy of small composable tools, and the startup-within-a-corporation model.

candidates.name: Building Complex
candidates.description: A building should be conceived as a complex of smaller buildings, not a monolith. The architectural argument against monolithic systems, anticipating modular architecture and service-oriented design.

candidates.name: Circulation Realms
candidates.description: Organize circulation into nested realms of increasing privacy. Maps to network segmentation, routing hierarchies, and the layered architecture pattern -- traffic flows through progressively more specific domains.

candidates.name: Family of Entrances
candidates.description: A complex of buildings needs a family of entrances, not one grand entrance and many back doors. Maps to multiple API endpoints, polyglot interfaces, and the principle that different users need different entry points.

candidates.name: Site Repair
candidates.description: Build on the worst part of the site, preserve the best. Maps to refactoring strategy -- improve the weakest code first, don't rewrite what already works. The brownfield development philosophy.

candidates.name: Positive Outdoor Space
candidates.description: Outdoor space should be shaped, not leftover. The negative space between buildings matters as much as the buildings. Maps to API surface design, whitespace in UI, and the principle that the gaps between components are design decisions too.

candidates.name: Wings of Light
candidates.description: Keep buildings narrow so natural light reaches every room. Maps to the single-responsibility principle and the argument that wide, deep modules are harder to illuminate (understand) than narrow, shallow ones.

candidates.name: Connected Buildings
candidates.description: Buildings should be physically connected, not isolated. Maps to service mesh architecture, integration patterns, and the principle that isolated systems create organizational silos.

candidates.name: Main Entrance
candidates.description: A building's main entrance should be visible, obvious, and welcoming. Maps to API entry points, landing pages, main() functions, and the principle that a system's primary interface should be discoverable without a map.

candidates.name: Half-Hidden Garden
candidates.description: A garden should be partly visible from the street but not fully exposed. Maps to the principle of encapsulation with discoverability -- internal richness should be hinted at but not fully exposed.

candidates.name: Entrance Transition
candidates.description: The entrance to a building should create a transition between outside and inside. Maps to onboarding flows, login experiences, and the UX principle that context-switching requires a deliberate threshold.

candidates.name: Hierarchy of Open Space
candidates.description: Open spaces should form a hierarchy from large public to small private. Maps to information architecture, nested scoping in programming languages, and the organizational principle of cascading access levels.

candidates.name: Cascade of Roofs
candidates.description: A building should have a cascade of roof forms, not one flat roof. Maps to layered architecture, defense in depth, and the principle that a system's protective boundary should have depth and variety.

candidates.name: Sheltering Roof
candidates.description: The roof is the most fundamental element -- it shelters everything beneath it. Maps to platform layers, umbrella architectures, and the principle that the outermost boundary of a system defines its identity.

candidates.name: Paths and Goals
candidates.description: Paths should lead toward visible goals. Maps to user flow design, progressive disclosure in UIs, and the navigation principle that users need to see where they are going, not just where they are.

candidates.name: Something Roughly in the Middle
candidates.description: Every public space needs something in the middle to anchor it. Maps to the hub-and-spoke architecture, central registries, and the organizational principle that communities need a focal point.

candidates.name: Intimacy Gradient
candidates.description: Rooms should be arranged in a gradient from most public to most private. Maps to API visibility layers, progressive authentication, and the UX pattern of revealing complexity gradually.

candidates.name: Common Areas at the Heart
candidates.description: Place common areas at the center so everyone passes through. Maps to shared libraries, common infrastructure, and the organizational design of placing shared functions (platform teams) at the core.

candidates.name: The Flow Through Rooms
candidates.description: Rooms should flow into each other, not branch off corridors. Maps to data pipeline design, the chain-of-responsibility pattern, and the principle that processing steps should connect directly rather than through a central dispatcher.

candidates.name: Short Passages
candidates.description: Keep corridors short. Long passages are disorienting and impersonal. Maps to minimizing indirection in code, keeping call stacks shallow, and the principle that the path between intention and action should be short.

candidates.name: Staircase as a Stage
candidates.description: A staircase should be a place of social interaction, not just a way to change levels. Maps to the principle that transitions between abstraction layers should be visible and meaningful, not hidden infrastructure.

candidates.name: Zen View
candidates.description: Don't expose a beautiful view constantly -- reveal it through a narrow opening so it stays special. Maps to progressive disclosure in UX, the principle of information scarcity, and the design choice to hide complexity until it's needed.

candidates.name: Tapestry of Light and Dark
candidates.description: A building needs alternating areas of light and dark. Maps to the rhythm of high-activity and low-activity zones in UIs, work/rest cycles in systems, and the principle that contrast creates comprehensibility.

candidates.name: A Room of One's Own
candidates.description: Every person needs a private space they control. Maps to personal workspaces in development (local environments), individual autonomy in organizations, and the namespace-per-developer pattern.

candidates.name: Flexible Office Space
candidates.description: Office space should be rearrangeable. Maps to configurable systems, feature flags, and the organizational principle that structures should adapt to changing work rather than forcing work into fixed structures.

candidates.name: Small Work Groups
candidates.description: Work groups should be small (5-20 people) and self-managing. Directly anticipates agile teams, two-pizza teams, and the scaling principle that large organizations should be composed of small autonomous groups.

candidates.name: A Place to Wait
candidates.description: Wherever people must wait, design the waiting space with care. Maps to loading states, queue management, and the UX principle that waiting is a design problem, not just an engineering problem.

candidates.name: Half-Private Office
candidates.description: An office should be partly open and partly enclosed. Maps to the open-source model (public repo, private deployment), hybrid work arrangements, and the information-sharing principle of selective transparency.

candidates.name: Open Stairs
candidates.description: Stairs should be open, visible, and inviting -- not hidden in fire towers. Maps to making abstraction layers visible and navigable, transparent escalation paths in organizations, and the argument against hidden complexity.

candidates.name: Light on Two Sides of Every Room
candidates.description: Rooms lit from only one side feel institutional. Maps to the principle that problems need multiple perspectives, code needs multiple reviewers, and understanding requires more than one source of illumination.

candidates.name: Building Edge
candidates.description: The most interesting activity happens at the edge where building meets street. Maps to edge computing, boundary objects in organizations, and the principle that innovation happens at interfaces between systems.

candidates.name: Street Windows
candidates.description: Windows on the street let people inside watch the world. Maps to observability dashboards, logging, and the monitoring principle that internal systems need windows onto external activity.

candidates.name: Connection to the Earth
candidates.description: Buildings should feel connected to the ground, not floating above it. Maps to grounded systems design -- staying close to the data, close to the user, close to the hardware. The argument against excessive abstraction.

candidates.name: Garden Growing Wild
candidates.description: The best gardens are slightly wild, not perfectly manicured. Maps to organic codebases, emergent architecture, and the principle that over-planning kills the life of a system.

candidates.name: Alcoves
candidates.description: Large rooms need smaller spaces within them. Maps to namespaces within modules, breakout rooms in meetings, and the principle that large undifferentiated spaces (codebases, organizations) need internal structure.

candidates.name: Window Place
candidates.description: A window should be a place to sit, not just a hole in the wall. Maps to the principle that interfaces between systems should be habitable spaces for work, not just data pass-throughs.

candidates.name: Workspace Enclosure
candidates.description: A workspace needs partial enclosure to feel like a place. Maps to the argument for private offices in software, the concept of flow state requiring boundaries, and the open-plan-office backlash.

candidates.name: Sitting Circle
candidates.description: Arrange seats in a circle so everyone faces each other. Maps to standup meetings, round-table discussions, and the organizational principle that hierarchy is encoded in spatial arrangement.

candidates.name: Ceiling Height Variety
candidates.description: Vary ceiling heights to match the social function of each room. Maps to the principle that different types of work need different environments -- detail views vs. dashboards, focused work vs. creative brainstorming.

candidates.name: Windows Overlooking Life
candidates.description: Windows should look onto human activity, not blank walls. Maps to dashboards showing real user behavior, production monitoring, and the principle that systems should observe living systems, not synthetic test data.

candidates.name: Thick Walls
candidates.description: Walls should be thick enough to contain storage, seats, and alcoves. Maps to rich interfaces between modules, middleware layers, and the principle that boundaries between systems should contain useful functionality, not just be thin separators.

candidates.name: Secret Place
candidates.description: Every house needs a secret place where children (and adults) can hide. Maps to Easter eggs in software, hidden developer menus, and the principle that systems benefit from small, undocumented delights.

candidates.name: Structure Follows Social Spaces
candidates.description: The structural system of a building should follow its social spaces, not the other way around. Anticipates Conway's Law and the inverse Conway maneuver -- system architecture should follow team structure and human needs, not impose structure on them.

candidates.name: Good Materials
candidates.description: Use materials that age well and can be repaired. Maps to choosing proven technology stacks, avoiding dependencies that won't be maintained, and the 'boring technology' argument.

candidates.name: Gradual Stiffening
candidates.description: Don't make the structure rigid from the start -- let it stiffen gradually as the design becomes clear. Maps to iterative development, prototyping, and the agile principle of deferring commitment until the last responsible moment.

candidates.name: Natural Doors and Windows
candidates.description: Place doors and windows where they naturally want to be, based on how the room is used. Maps to the principle that APIs should follow natural usage patterns, not arbitrary conventions -- affordance-driven interface design.

candidates.name: Deep Reveals
candidates.description: Window reveals should be deep enough to create a sense of thickness and shelter. Maps to rich error messages, detailed API documentation, and the principle that the boundary between inside and outside should carry information, not just mark a line.

candidates.name: Filtered Light
candidates.description: Use translucent materials to filter light. Maps to data filtering, abstraction layers that let some information through while blocking noise, and the middleware pattern.

candidates.name: Small Panes
candidates.description: Use small window panes rather than large sheets of glass. Maps to the principle of small, composable UI components, microcommits, and the argument that small pieces are more human-scaled than monolithic surfaces.

candidates.name: Ornament
candidates.description: Ornament is not decoration -- it is the finishing that makes a building feel complete. Maps to polish in software, the difference between 'works' and 'feels right,' and the argument that craft beyond function matters.

candidates.name: Pools of Light
candidates.description: Light a room with pools of light over task areas, not uniform overhead light. Maps to focused attention, spotlight-style UI highlighting, and the principle that emphasis should be selective, not uniform.

candidates.name: Different Chairs
candidates.description: A room needs different kinds of chairs for different moods and activities. Maps to multiple interface modes, accessibility options, and the principle that one-size-fits-all design serves no one well.

candidates.name: Things From Your Life
candidates.description: Fill your home with things that have personal meaning. Maps to customizable workspaces, personal dotfiles, and the principle that tools become extensions of identity through personalization.

candidates.name: Piecemeal Growth
candidates.description: Growth should be incremental and organic, not master-planned. From Alexander's broader philosophy (The Oregon Experiment). Maps to agile, iterative development, and the argument against big-bang rewrites.
candidates.note: Not one of the 253 numbered patterns but core Alexander concept. Already exists in catalog.

candidates.name: The Quality Without a Name
candidates.description: The essential quality that makes a building alive, from The Timeless Way of Building. Maps to software habitability, code that 'feels right,' and the aesthetic dimension of engineering quality.
candidates.note: From The Timeless Way of Building, not A Pattern Language. Already exists in catalog.

candidates.name: Pattern Language as Shared Vocabulary
candidates.description: The concept of pattern language itself -- the idea that a shared vocabulary of named solutions enables collaborative design. Meta-metaphor from Alexander's work.
candidates.note: Meta-level concept, not a numbered pattern. Already exists in catalog.

candidates.name: Software Habitability
candidates.description: Richard Gabriel's extension of Alexander: code should be habitable, comfortable to live in and work with over time.
candidates.note: Gabriel's extension of Alexander, not a numbered pattern. Already exists in catalog.
